etymology: From the Old English wæcce, “a waking, a keeping guard,” kin to wake and watch; a “watch” of the night is the span for which a sentinel stood his post. Hebrew reckoning knew three such divisions of the dark; the Roman, four.
biblical_def: A watch of the night is one of its appointed divisions — not the darkness itself, but a guarded portion of it, the span for which a sentinel stood his post before the next relieved him. The modern ear hears “night” as one unbroken block; the Scripture divides it. Israel of old kept three watches — hence Gideon came “in the beginning of the middle watch” (Jdg 7:19), and it was “in the morning watch” that the LORD looked through the pillar of fire and troubled the Egyptians (Exo 14:24). Jeremiah bids stricken Zion cry “in the beginning of the watches” (Lam 2:19). By our Lord’s day Rome had imposed four, and the Gospel names them in order: “at even, or at midnight, or at the cockcrowing, or in the morning.” It was in the last of these that Christ came upon the water: “in the fourth watch of the night Jesus went unto them, walking on the sea” (Mat 14:25) — the coldest watch, when the disciples had toiled all night and were spent, and He came. The watches are the believer’s hours of prayer: “When I remember thee upon my bed, and meditate on thee in the night watches” (Psa 63:6). And they measure a mercy, for to the LORD who never sleeps a thousand years “are but as yesterday when it is past, and as a watch in the night” (Psa 90:4).
webster_summary: One of the divisions of the night during which a sentinel kept guard — three by Hebrew reckoning, four by Roman.
webster_full: WATCH, a division of the night; the period during which a sentinel or guard is on duty.
From Old English wæcce, a waking, a keeping guard through the dark hours.
The Hebrews parted the night into three watches; the Romans into four.
Christ came to the labouring disciples in the fourth watch of the night (Mat 14:25).
The godly remember God and pour out prayer in the night watches (Psa 63:6).
scriptures: Lam 2:19

Arise, cry out in the night: in the beginning of the watches pour out thine heart like water before the face of the Lord: lift up thy hands toward him for the life of thy young children, that faint for hunger in the top of every street.
Psa 63:6
When I remember thee upon my bed, and meditate on thee in the night watches.
Psa 90:4
For a thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday when it is past, and as a watch in the night.
And in the fourth watch of the night Jesus went unto them, walking on the sea.
corruption_summary: Not a poetic synonym for “night,” but its ordered divisions; the word recovers the dark hours as a season of appointed watch and prayer.
corruption_paragraphs: The honest drift to name here is the flattening of the phrase. A modern reader, meeting “the night watches,” hears only a soft word for the dark and misses the ordered thing the Scripture means. A watch was a shift — a fixed span with a beginning and an end, when a man stood armed against whatever the night might bring, and was relieved by another when his turn was done. To lose the word is to lose the picture: the changing of the guard, the trumpet at the middle watch, the LORD looking down in the morning watch upon a drowning enemy. The night is not one undivided weight; it is measured, manned, and kept.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the night as a season of watch. The saint is not to sleep out the dark like the world, but to keep his post in it — to remember God upon his bed and meditate on Him in the night watches, to arise in the beginning of the watches and pour out his heart like water before the face of the Lord. The longest night has its divisions, and each has its duty; and over the whole of it stands the God to whom a thousand years are but a single watch. The believer keeps his watch because his Keeper never sleeps.
roots_summary: The word means one of the guarded divisions of the night, the span of a sentinel’s duty.
roots_lines: Watch — Old English wæcce, “a waking, a keeping guard.”
A watch of the night is the span for which a sentinel stood his post.
The Hebrews kept three watches; the Romans divided the night into four.
The four are named at even, midnight, cockcrowing, and morning (Mar 13:35).
Christ walked the sea in the fourth watch, and the LORD saw in the morning watch (Exo 14:24).
usage: Watches of the night are its divisions, not a mere word for the dark — each a shift with its own duty.
Christ came in the fourth watch, when the rowers were spent: the darkest watch is not beyond His reach.
David meditated in the night watches: the believer keeps his post while the world sleeps.

etymology: From cock (the male fowl) + crowing (its cry) — the crowing of the cock before dawn. In the Roman division of the night it named the third watch, running roughly from midnight to about three in the morning, just before the day broke.
biblical_def: Cockcrowing is the third watch of the night by Roman reckoning — the hours before dawn, named for the cock that cries as the dark thins toward morning. Our Lord sets it among the four watches when He charges His own to be ready: “Watch ye therefore: for ye know not when the master of the house cometh, at even, or at midnight, or at the cockcrowing, or in the morning” (Mar 13:35). But the word carries a heavier freight than the clock, for it is bound forever to Peter’s fall. At the supper the Lord foretold it exactly: “That this day, even in this night, before the cock crow twice, thou shalt deny me thrice” (Mar 14:30). Peter, sure of his own strength, would not believe it; the other Gospels record the same warning in its barest form — “before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice” (Mat 26:34) — and John gives the Lord’s searching question and its sentence: “Wilt thou lay down thy life for my sake? Verily, verily, I say unto thee, The cock shall not crow, till thou hast denied me thrice” (Joh 13:38). And so it fell out: the cock crew, and Peter remembered, and went out and wept bitterly. The cockcrowing is therefore a mercy as well as a measure of the night. It is the appointed sound by which the Lord recalled a fallen disciple to himself — the ordinary crowing of a barnyard bird made the instrument of a sovereign grace that would not let Peter perish in his sin, but broke his heart and brought him back.
webster_summary: The crowing of the cock before dawn; the third of the four Roman watches of the night, just before morning.
webster_full: COCKCROWING, the time when the cock crows; the watch before dawn.
From cock, the male fowl, and crowing, its cry at the approach of day.
In the Roman night it named the third watch, from about midnight to the morning.
Christ names it among the watches at which the master may come (Mar 13:35).
At the cockcrowing Peter denied his Lord thrice, as was foretold (Mar 14:30).
scriptures: Watch ye therefore: for ye know not when the master of the house cometh, at even, or at midnight, or at the cockcrowing, or in the morning:
And Jesus saith unto him, Verily I say unto thee, That this day, even in this night, before the cock crow twice, thou shalt deny me thrice.
Jesus said unto him, Verily I say unto thee, That this night, before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice.
Jesus answered him, Wilt thou lay down thy life for my sake? Verily, verily, I say unto thee, The cock shall not crow, till thou hast denied me thrice.
corruption_summary: The watch before dawn, and the hour of Peter’s fall; the word recovers watchfulness and the mercy that recalls a stumbling saint.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern reader, meeting “the cockcrowing,” hears a quaint noise of the farmyard and does not know he has been given the name of a watch. It was the third division of the night, the cold hours before the day, and our Lord names it as one of the times the master of the house may return: watch ye therefore, for ye know not when he cometh. The command is not a mood but an office. The servant does not choose the watch in which his lord will come; he keeps every watch as though it were the one. To lose the word is to soften the warning, as though vigilance were a feeling; the Scripture makes it a post to be manned through the dark.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the mercy folded into the crowing. Peter, warned in plain words, trusted his own resolve and denied his Lord thrice before the cock had finished the watch. Yet the very sound that convicted him was appointed for his recovery: the cock crew, and he remembered the word of Jesus, and wept bitterly. Here is the difference between Peter and Judas — both fell, but grace had prayed for one that his faith fail not, and an ordinary bird’s cry was the sovereign summons that broke his heart and turned him home. The cockcrowing preaches that the Lord keeps watch over His own even in the watch of their fall.
roots_summary: The word means the crowing of the cock, and so the pre-dawn watch of the Roman night.
roots_lines: Cockcrowing — from cock, the male fowl, and its crowing at dawn.
It named the third of the four Roman watches, before the morning broke.
Christ sets it among the hours the master of the house may come (Mar 13:35).
Before the cock should crow, Peter would deny his Lord thrice (Mat 26:34).
The cock crew, and the fallen disciple remembered, and wept bitterly.
usage: Cockcrowing is the third watch, not merely a barnyard sound: the hours before the day.
At the cockcrowing the master may come: keep every watch as though it were the last.
The cock crew and Peter remembered — the appointed sound of a sovereign mercy.

etymology: From the Old English æfentid — æfen, “evening,” and tid, “time, season” (the older sense of tide, as in “Whitsuntide”). Hence simply evening-time; it has nothing to do with the tide of the sea.
biblical_def: Eventide means evening-time — the tide here is the old word for a season or hour, not the flood of the sea. It is the close of the day, the cool turning of afternoon into night, and Scripture fills it with meaning. It is the hour of meditation: “And Isaac went out to meditate in the field at the eventide” (Gen 24:63), and while he prayed, unknowing, the LORD was bringing Rebekah to him over the hills — providence arriving at the very hour the servant sought the Lord’s face. It is the hour our Saviour surveyed His Father’s house: “when he had looked round about upon all things, and now the eventide was come, he went out unto Bethany with the twelve” (Mar 11:11) — the King had come to His temple and marked its every corruption before He cleansed it on the morrow. It is the hour of the first persecution: they laid hands on Peter and John “and put them in hold unto the next day: for it was now eventide” (Act 4:3), the day of preaching Christ risen ending in a prison cell. And it is an hour of sudden judgment upon the enemies of God’s people: “And behold at eveningtide trouble; and before the morning he is not” (Isa 17:14) — the spoiler flourishing at dusk and gone by dawn. Eventide gathers up the day’s labour into rest, its worship into meditation, and its threatenings into the hand of a God who works while His servants sleep.
webster_summary: Evening-time; the close of the day — the tide being the old word for a season, not the sea’s flood.
webster_full: EVENTIDE, the time of evening; the close of the day, toward nightfall.
From Old English æfen, “evening,” and tid, “time, season.”
The tide is the old sense of time, as in “Whitsuntide,” not the sea.
Isaac went out to meditate in the field at the eventide (Gen 24:63).
Christ surveyed the temple when the eventide was come (Mar 11:11).
scriptures: And Isaac went out to meditate in the field at the eventide: and he lifted up his eyes, and saw, and, behold, the camels were coming.
And Jesus entered into Jerusalem, and into the temple: and when he had looked round about upon all things, and now the eventide was come, he went out unto Bethany with the twelve.
Act 4:3
And they laid hands on them, and put them in hold unto the next day: for it was now eventide.
And behold at eveningtide trouble; and before the morning he is not. This is the portion of them that spoil us, and the lot of them that rob us.
corruption_summary: Evening-time, not a sea-tide; the word recovers the close of day as an hour of meditation, worship, and the quiet working of providence.
corruption_paragraphs: The honest misreading here is the pull of the wrong tide. The modern ear hears “eventide” and half-imagines the sea — some evening flood upon a shore — when the word means nothing of the kind. Tide is the older English for a time or season, the same root that gives us “Whitsuntide” and “noontide”; eventide is simply the eventime, the hour of the day’s decline. Once the word is heard rightly, the texts open. Isaac walked out at the eventime to pray; Christ looked upon the temple at the eventime; the apostles were jailed at the eventime. The word marks the hinge of the day, when labour ceases and the heart turns homeward and heavenward.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the sanctity of the day’s close. Scripture makes the eventide an hour of meditation and of providence — Isaac went out to meditate in the field, and lifted up his eyes to see his bride approaching; while he sought the LORD, the LORD was already answering. The evening is the natural altar of the day, when a man reckons with what the hours have held and commits the night to God. And it is a witness against the enemy’s security, for the spoiler is at ease at eventide and undone before morning. Let the believer close his day as Isaac closed his: in the field, at prayer, with his eyes lifted to see what God is bringing over the hill.
roots_summary: The word means evening-time, the close of the day — tide in its old sense of season.
roots_lines: Eventide — Old English æfen (“evening”) + tid (“time”).
The tide is the older word for a season, as in Whitsuntide, not the sea.
It names the close of the day, the cool turning toward night.
Isaac meditated at the eventide, and saw his bride coming (Gen 24:63).
Christ viewed the temple at eventide before cleansing it (Mar 11:11).
usage: Eventide is evening-time, not a sea-tide: the tide is the old word for a season.
Isaac went out to meditate at the eventide — and providence met him in the field.
The eventide was come, and the King, having marked all, went out to Bethany.

etymology: A rendering of the Jewish reckoning of the daylight hours, counted from sunrise: the “third hour” is roughly nine in the morning, three hours after the day began. The hours of the night were counted likewise, from sunset.
biblical_def: The third hour is nine o’clock in the morning by the reckoning of Scripture, which numbered the twelve daylight hours from sunrise. It is not our third hour but the third after dawn, and the modern reader who forgets the difference will misplace every clock in the Gospels. Peter appeals to it on the day of Pentecost, answering the charge of drunkenness: “these are not drunken, as ye suppose, seeing it is but the third hour of the day” (Act 2:15) — too early for wine, and so the tongues of fire must be owned as the promised Spirit and not the fruit of the cup. It is an hour of labour in the Lord’s parable of the vineyard: the householder “went out about the third hour, and saw others standing idle in the marketplace” (Mat 20:3), and hired them into his field — a picture of the free call of grace at every hour of the day. And it is the hour of the crucifixion in Mark’s plain account: “And it was the third hour, and they crucified him” (Mar 15:25) — the Lamb of God nailed up at the morning hour of the temple sacrifice. The hours of the night were counted the same way from sunset, as when the chief captain readied his soldiers for Paul “at the third hour of the night” (Act 23:23). So the third hour teaches the reader to keep Scripture’s own clock: nine in the morning, when the Spirit fell, when the labourers were called, and when the Son of God was lifted up.
webster_summary: Nine o’clock in the morning by the Jewish reckoning, which counted the twelve daylight hours from sunrise.
webster_full: THIRD HOUR, the third hour after sunrise; about nine in the morning.
Scripture numbered the twelve hours of daylight from dawn, not from midnight.
The hours of the night were likewise counted from sunset (Act 23:23).
Peter says it is but the third hour, too early for drunkenness (Act 2:15).
It was the third hour when they crucified the Lord (Mar 15:25).
scriptures: Act 2:15
For these are not drunken, as ye suppose, seeing it is but the third hour of the day.
And it was the third hour, and they crucified him.
Mat 20:3
And he went out about the third hour, and saw others standing idle in the marketplace,
And he called unto him two centurions, saying, Make ready two hundred soldiers to go to Caesarea, and horsemen threescore and ten, and spearmen two hundred, at the third hour of the night;
corruption_summary: Nine in the morning, not our third hour; the word recovers Scripture’s own clock, reckoned from sunrise and sunset.
corruption_paragraphs: The honest error to correct is the imported clock. A modern reader hears “the third hour” and thinks of three in the morning or three by his own watch, and so the day of the Gospels comes apart in his hands. Scripture counts the twelve hours of light from sunrise: the third hour is about nine in the forenoon, the sixth is noon, the ninth is three in the afternoon, and the hours of the night run likewise from sunset. Keep that clock and the accounts fall into order — Peter’s crowd is charged with drunkenness at nine in the morning, and he answers that the hour itself refutes them; the labourers are hired through the working day; the darkness at the crucifixion falls from the sixth hour to the ninth, noon to mid-afternoon.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the ordered day under God. Scripture’s hours are not vague; they are marked, and the marking matters. At the third hour the Holy Ghost was poured out and the Church was born; at the third hour, by Mark’s reckoning, the Lord was crucified; at the third hour the householder went out to call the idle into his vineyard. The hours of prayer were kept — Peter and John went up to the temple at the ninth hour, the hour of prayer (Act 3:1). A people that keeps no hours keeps no watch; the God who appointed the sun to rule the day appointed its hours too, and filled them with His works.
roots_summary: The word means nine in the morning, the third of the twelve daylight hours counted from sunrise.
roots_lines: Third hour — the third hour after sunrise, about nine in the forenoon.
Scripture counts the twelve hours of daylight from dawn, not from midnight.
The hours of the night were reckoned the same way, from sunset (Act 23:23).
At the third hour the Spirit fell and Peter answered the charge (Act 2:15).
At the third hour, by Mark, the Lord Jesus was crucified (Mar 15:25).
usage: The third hour is nine in the morning, not our third hour: Scripture counts from sunrise.
It is but the third hour, said Peter — too early for wine, so own the Spirit instead.
It was the third hour, and they crucified him: the Lamb slain at the morning sacrifice.

etymology: A rabbinic measure of the distance a man might lawfully walk on the sabbath without breaking its rest — about two thousand cubits, some three-quarters of a mile. It was reckoned from the command that no man go out of his place on the seventh day, joined to the two thousand cubits of the Levite suburbs.
biblical_def: A sabbath day’s journey is the short distance the rabbis allowed a man to travel on the day of rest without breaking it — about two thousand cubits, a little under a mile. The phrase occurs once, and it marks the place of the Ascension: the disciples “returned they unto Jerusalem from the mount called Olivet, which is from Jerusalem a sabbath day’s journey” (Act 1:12). Luke measures the holy hill by the compass of the law: Olivet stood within the walk a devout man might take on the sabbath. The measure itself was built from two texts. The command gave the principle of rest in place: “abide ye every man in his place, let no man go out of his place on the seventh day” (Exo 16:29) — the sabbath was not for wandering but for staying, resting, worshipping. And the figure of two thousand cubits was drawn from the suburbs of the Levite cities: “ye shall measure from without the city on the east side two thousand cubits” (Num 35:5), and from the space Israel kept between themselves and the ark, “about two thousand cubits by measure”. The rabbis fenced the day about with such reckonings, and often the fence became a snare, straining at the cubit while the heart wandered far. Yet the principle under the fence is holy and abiding: the sabbath is a bounded rest, a day to abide in one’s place before the LORD. “Bear no burden on the sabbath day” (Jer 17:21), He said — not to bind the feet, but to free the soul for Himself.
webster_summary: The distance a Jew might lawfully walk on the sabbath — about two thousand cubits, some three-quarters of a mile.
webster_full: SABBATH DAY'S JOURNEY, the distance a man might travel on the sabbath without breach of its rest.
Reckoned by the rabbis at about two thousand cubits, near three-quarters of a mile.
Drawn from the command to abide in one’s place on the seventh day (Exo 16:29).
The two thousand cubits came from the Levite suburbs and the space before the ark (Num 35:5).
Olivet lay a sabbath day’s journey from Jerusalem (Act 1:12).
scriptures: Act 1:12
Then returned they unto Jerusalem from the mount called Olivet, which is from Jerusalem a sabbath day's journey.
See, for that the LORD hath given you the sabbath, therefore he giveth you on the sixth day the bread of two days; abide ye every man in his place, let no man go out of his place on the seventh day.
Num 35:5

And ye shall measure from without the city on the east side two thousand cubits, and on the south side two thousand cubits, and on the west side two thousand cubits, and on the north side two thousand cubits; and the city shall be in the midst: this shall be to them the suburbs of the cities.
Thus saith the LORD; Take heed to yourselves, and bear no burden on the sabbath day, nor bring it in by the gates of Jerusalem;
corruption_summary: The rabbinic limit on sabbath travel; the word recovers the bounded rest of the day, and warns against fencing the law until the fence becomes the burden.
corruption_paragraphs: The phrase opens a window on how the rabbis kept the sabbath — and on how such keeping could go wrong. The two thousand cubits were a fence about the command, a way of measuring obedience by the pace; and there is honest wisdom in it, for the LORD did say, abide every man in his place, let no man go out of his place on the seventh day. But a fence measured in cubits is easily turned into a snare. The same tradition that reckoned the sabbath day’s journey learned to sell the poor for silver and yet strain at a step too many, tithing mint and cummin while it omitted the weightier matters. Our Lord, who is Lord of the sabbath, healed on that day and let His disciples pluck the ears, and rebuked the men who had made the day of rest into a day of burdens.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the bounded rest itself, not the abolition of it. The sabbath was given — the LORD hath given you the sabbath — and it was given as a mercy: a day to abide in one’s place, to bear no burden, to cease from labour and be filled with God. The abuse of the rabbis was to multiply the fences; the abuse of our age is to tear them all down and keep no day at all. Both lose the gift. The Christian sabbath is not two thousand cubits chalked upon the ground, but a whole day set apart for the worship and the rest of the people of God, a foretaste of the rest that remaineth. The measure was a fence; the day is a feast.
roots_summary: The word means the short distance a Jew might walk on the sabbath, about two thousand cubits.
roots_lines: Sabbath day's journey — the lawful walk of the day of rest.
Reckoned at about two thousand cubits, near three-quarters of a mile.
Founded on the command to abide in one’s place on the seventh day (Exo 16:29).
The two thousand cubits came from the Levite suburbs (Num 35:5).
Olivet stood a sabbath day’s journey from Jerusalem (Act 1:12).
usage: A sabbath day’s journey was about two thousand cubits: Olivet lay within that walk of the city.
The measure fenced the day of rest — abide every man in his place on the seventh day.
The rabbis chalked the cubits; the Lord of the sabbath gave the day as a mercy, not a burden.

etymology: From the Latin deputare, “to assign, to appoint,” through the Old French deputé; hence one appointed to act for another. In the KJV it renders the Greek anthupatos, the Roman proconsul — the governor set over a senatorial province in the emperor’s stead.
biblical_def: A deputy in the KJV is a Roman proconsul — the governor set over a province to rule in the emperor’s stead. The modern ear hears “deputy” as an underling, a sheriff’s second; but the Authorized Version means the highest civil officer of a senatorial province, a man of consular rank. Luke, who wrote when such titles could be checked and mistaken at peril, uses the word with exactness. On Cyprus the gospel came “with the deputy of the country, Sergius Paulus, a prudent man; who called for Barnabas and Saul, and desired to hear the word of God” (Act 13:7); and when Elymas the sorcerer withstood them and was struck blind, “then the deputy, when he saw what was done, believed, being astonished at the doctrine of the Lord” (Act 13:12) — a proconsul of Rome brought to Christ. At Corinth another deputy stayed the malice of the Jews: “when Gallio was the deputy of Achaia, the Jews made insurrection with one accord against Paul” (Act 18:12), and Gallio drove the accusers from his judgment seat. And the town clerk of Ephesus stilled a riot by pointing to the office: “the law is open, and there are deputies: let them implead one another” (Act 19:38). The word even reaches back into the Old Testament, where Edom under Judah’s hand had no king of its own: “there was then no king in Edom: a deputy was king” (1Ki 22:47). Everywhere the deputy is the ordained authority of the higher power — and Scripture shows that authority, again and again, made the servant of the gospel’s advance.
webster_summary: One appointed to act for another; in the KJV, a Roman proconsul, the governor of a province.
webster_full: DEPUTY, one appointed to exercise an office in another’s stead; a lieutenant, a viceregent.
From Latin deputare, “to appoint”; through Old French deputé.
In the KJV it renders the Greek anthupatos, the Roman proconsul.
Sergius Paulus the deputy of Cyprus believed the doctrine of the Lord (Act 13:12).
Gallio the deputy of Achaia refused to judge Paul’s accusers (Act 18:12).
scriptures: Act 13:7
Which was with the deputy of the country, Sergius Paulus, a prudent man; who called for Barnabas and Saul, and desired to hear the word of God.
And when Gallio was the deputy of Achaia, the Jews made insurrection with one accord against Paul, and brought him to the judgment seat,
Wherefore if Demetrius, and the craftsmen which are with him, have a matter against any man, the law is open, and there are deputies: let them implead one another.
There was then no king in Edom: a deputy was king.
corruption_summary: Not an underling but a proconsul, the governor of a province; the word recovers Rome’s highest provincial officer and the ordained authority he bore.
corruption_paragraphs: The honest drift here is a shrinking of the office. In modern speech a deputy is a subordinate — a deputy sheriff, a deputy manager, the man a rank below. In the Authorized Version the deputy is the proconsul, the supreme civil governor of a Roman province, answerable to the Senate and to Caesar and to no one nearer. Sergius Paulus ruled Cyprus; Gallio ruled Achaia; these were not clerks but rulers, men who bore the sword. To read the word as our own lowers the whole account and hides the marvel of it: that Rome’s great provincial governors were brought within hearing of the gospel, and one of them, astonished at the doctrine of the Lord, believed.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition in the word itself, yet it opens a doctrine our age needs and must be named plainly: the deputy’s authority was from God. Paul, who stood before more than one of them, wrote that the powers that be are ordained of God, and that the ruler is the minister of God for good. Against the anarchic temper that despises all rule, Scripture sets the ordinance of the magistrate; against the statolatry that makes the ruler a god, it sets the truth that he is a deputy — appointed, accountable, a servant of a higher throne. Gallio and Sergius Paulus held real power, but they held it in trust from the King of kings, whose gospel used their very courts and provinces to run its course. The Christian honours the deputy because God ordained the office, and fears the God who will one day judge every deputy He appointed.
roots_summary: The word means one appointed to act for another; in the KJV, a Roman proconsul or provincial governor.
roots_lines: Deputy — Latin deputare, “to appoint,” via Old French deputé.
It renders the Greek anthupatos, the Roman proconsul.
Not a subordinate, but the supreme civil governor of a province.
Sergius Paulus, deputy of Cyprus, believed the word (Act 13:7).
Even Edom under Judah had a deputy for a king (1Ki 22:47).
usage: A deputy in the KJV is a proconsul, not an underling: Gallio was the deputy of all Achaia.
The deputy of Cyprus, astonished at the doctrine of the Lord, believed — a governor won to Christ.
The law is open, and there are deputies: the ruler’s court, not the mob, is God’s ordinance.

etymology: From the Latin serviens, “one serving,” through the Old French sergent; hence an officer who serves a court or magistrate. In the KJV it renders the Roman lictor — the attendant who bore the fasces and executed the magistrate’s sentence.
biblical_def: A serjeant in the KJV is a Roman lictor — the officer who attended a magistrate, bore before him the bundled rods and axe of his authority, and carried out his commands of arrest, scourging, and release. It is not the sergeant of a modern army. The word belongs to the story of Philippi, where Paul and Silas were beaten and jailed without trial. When the magistrates, alarmed at the earthquake and the jailer’s report, wished to be rid of their prisoners quietly, “the magistrates sent the serjeants, saying, Let those men go” (Act 16:35). But Paul would not slink out by a side door: they had beaten Romans openly and uncondemned, and should fetch them openly. “And the serjeants told these words unto the magistrates: and they feared, when they heard that they were Romans” (Act 16:38). The same officers who had earlier stood by as “the magistrates rent off their clothes, and commanded to beat them” (Act 16:22) now came trembling to escort them out. The serjeant is the visible edge of the magistrate’s power, the hand that holds the rod — and Scripture teaches that this power, rightly used, is God’s own ordinance: “he is the minister of God to thee for good… for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil” (Rom 13:4). The lictor’s rods at Philippi were wielded unjustly against innocent men, and the magistrates learned to fear; but the office itself, the bearing of the sword under authority, is appointed of God.
webster_summary: An officer who serves a court or magistrate; in the KJV, a Roman lictor, bearer of the rods of office.
webster_full: SERJEANT, an officer who attends a magistrate or court to execute its commands.
From Latin serviens, “one serving,” through Old French sergent.
In the KJV it renders the Roman lictor, who bore the fasces of office.
The magistrates of Philippi sent the serjeants to release Paul and Silas (Act 16:35).
The serjeants brought back word, and the magistrates feared (Act 16:38).
scriptures: And when it was day, the magistrates sent the serjeants, saying, Let those men go.
And the serjeants told these words unto the magistrates: and they feared, when they heard that they were Romans.
And the multitude rose up together against them: and the magistrates rent off their clothes, and commanded to beat them.
Rom 13:4

For he is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil.
corruption_summary: Not a military sergeant but a Roman lictor, the magistrate’s officer; the word recovers the lawful bearing of the sword under authority.
corruption_paragraphs: The honest confusion here is with the modern soldier. We hear “serjeant” and think of the drill-sergeant, the non-commissioned officer of an army; but the KJV means the lictor, the civil officer who walked before a Roman magistrate bearing the fasces — the bound rods and axe that were the very emblem of the power to scourge and to execute. At Philippi the serjeants were the hands that carried out the magistrates’ unjust sentence, and then the hands sent trembling to undo it. To read the word rightly is to see the machinery of Roman justice up close: the magistrate who commands, and the officer at his side who bears the rod and does the deed.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the sword borne under authority. The lictor’s rods are the very thing Paul has in view when he writes that the ruler beareth not the sword in vain, for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil. God has committed to the civil power a real and dreadful instrument, and the serjeant is that instrument in a man’s hand. At Philippi it was drawn against the innocent, and the magistrates were made to fear when they learned whom they had beaten; the abuse of the sword brings its own reckoning. Yet the office is holy, and the Christian neither despises it as the anarchist does nor worships it as the tyrant’s flatterer does. He honours the sword as God’s ordinance and trembles that it is not borne in vain.
roots_summary: The word means an officer serving a magistrate; in the KJV, a Roman lictor who bore the rods of office.
roots_lines: Serjeant — Latin serviens, “one serving,” via Old French sergent.
It renders the Roman lictor, attendant of the magistrate.
Not a military sergeant, but a civil officer bearing the fasces.
The serjeants were sent to release Paul from the Philippian jail (Act 16:35).
They feared when they learned they had beaten Romans (Act 16:38).
usage: A serjeant in the KJV is a lictor, not an army sergeant: the magistrate’s officer with the rods.
The magistrates sent the serjeants to let them go — but Paul demanded an open release.
The serjeant bears the rod: he beareth not the sword in vain, for he is God’s minister.

etymology: From town + clerk (Old English clerc, a clergyman or scholar, from the Latin clericus, and so a man of letters, a scribe). Hence the city’s recorder or scribe — in Ephesus, the chief civic officer who kept its records and answered to Rome for its order.
biblical_def: The townclerk of Scripture is no petty parish clerk but the chief recorder of a great city — at Ephesus, the officer who kept the public archives, presided over the assembly, and stood answerable to Rome for the peace of the place. The word occurs once, at the height of the riot Demetrius the silversmith had stirred against Paul, when the theatre had roared for two hours, “Great is Diana of the Ephesians.” Into that uproar stepped one man with the authority to quell it: “And when the townclerk had appeased the people, he said, Ye men of Ephesus” (Act 19:35). He reasoned with them like a magistrate: the city’s honour was not in danger, the accused had robbed no temple and blasphemed no goddess; if Demetrius had a cause, “the law is open, and there are deputies”; and the whole tumult imperilled them all, “for we are in danger to be called in question for this day’s uproar” (Act 19:40). He bade them “be quiet, and to do nothing rashly” (Act 19:36), and dismissed the assembly. Here a heathen officer, in the ordinary discharge of his office, became the shield of Christ’s servants against a mob. The whole scene preaches what Scripture teaches plainly: that civil order is God’s ordinance, that “the powers that be are ordained of God” (Rom 13:1), and that the believer is to “submit yourselves to every ordinance of man for the Lord’s sake” (1Pe 2:13). The townclerk kept the peace of Ephesus that day, and in keeping it he kept Paul.
webster_summary: The chief recorder or scribe of a city; at Ephesus, the officer who kept its records and answered to Rome for its order.
webster_full: TOWNCLERK, the recorder or scribe of a city; its chief civic officer of records and assembly.
From town and clerk, a man of letters, from Latin clericus.
At Ephesus he kept the archives and presided over the public assembly.
The townclerk appeased the people and stilled the riot for Diana (Act 19:35).
He warned them of danger and bade them do nothing rashly (Act 19:36).
scriptures: And when the townclerk had appeased the people, he said, Ye men of Ephesus, what man is there that knoweth not how that the city of the Ephesians is a worshipper of the great goddess Diana, and of the image which fell down from Jupiter?
Wherefore if Demetrius, and the craftsmen which are with him, have a matter against any man, the law is open, and there are deputies: let them implead one another.
Rom 13:1
Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.
Submit yourselves to every ordinance of man for the Lord's sake: whether it be to the king, as supreme;
corruption_summary: Not a lowly parish clerk but a city’s chief recorder; the word recovers the civic officer whose lawful order shielded Paul from the mob.
corruption_paragraphs: The honest shrinking of this word must be corrected. To modern ears a “town clerk” is a minor functionary, a keeper of licences at a small municipal desk; but the townclerk of Ephesus was the principal officer of one of the greatest cities of the empire, a man of standing before Rome, whose word could still a rioting theatre of thousands. The Greek names the keeper of the city’s records and the president of its assembly. When he rose and spoke, the crowd that had roared two hours for Diana fell silent and dispersed. To read him as a clerk of our own small towns is to miss the weight of the office and the wonder of the moment: the highest civic authority of Ephesus using his power to protect the messengers of the gospel.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the goodness of lawful order as God’s ordinance. The townclerk did nothing miraculous; he simply did his office — appeased the people, pointed the aggrieved to the open law and the deputies, warned of the danger of tumult, and dismissed the assembly. And by that ordinary discharge of a lawful office, God shielded His servants. The powers that be are ordained of God, and the Christian is to submit to every ordinance of man for the Lord’s sake, honouring even a heathen officer who keeps the peace. The mob is the enemy of the gospel’s free course; lawful order is its friend. God who rules the hearts of kings ruled the townclerk of Ephesus that day, and turned a pagan magistrate into a wall about Paul.
roots_summary: The word means the recorder or scribe of a city, its chief civic officer of records and assembly.
roots_lines: Townclerk — town + clerk (Latin clericus, a scholar, a scribe).

He pointed the aggrieved to the open law and the deputies (Act 19:38).
usage: The townclerk of Ephesus was the city’s chief recorder, not a small municipal clerk.
When the townclerk had appeased the people, the mob that roared for Diana fell quiet.
A pagan officer, doing his office, became God’s wall about Paul: the powers are ordained of God.

etymology: From the Old French chambrelenc, “officer of the chamber,” from Latin camera, “a chamber, a vaulted room”; hence the officer over a king’s private rooms, and by extension a court steward or the treasurer who kept the public purse (the “chamber” of the treasury).
biblical_def: A chamberlain is an officer of the chamber — in Scripture, either a great man’s household steward, or the treasurer who kept a city’s or a kingdom’s purse. The modern reader, if the word means anything to him, pictures a ceremonial court title; the KJV means a real officer of trust, near the seat of power. It is the man who governed access to a king: when Tyre and Sidon sought peace with Herod, they “having made Blastus the king’s chamberlain their friend, desired peace” (Act 12:20) — to reach the king one must first win the chamberlain. It is a keeper of the treasury, and one such was a brother in Christ: “Erastus the chamberlain of the city saluteth you” (Rom 16:23), a man of civic rank numbered among the saints at Corinth. It is an officer even in the idolatry of Judah’s kings, as at the reform of Josiah, who burned the sun-chariots “by the chamber of Nathanmelech the chamberlain, which was in the suburbs” (2Ki 23:11). And it is the ring of eunuch-chamberlains about a Persian throne: Ahasuerus commanded “the seven chamberlains that served in the presence of Ahasuerus the king” (Est 1:10) to bring Vashti before his drunken feast. In every case the chamberlain stands close to earthly majesty, holding its keys and its coin. Yet Scripture quietly reminds us that the highest chamberlain serves a dying king, while the least believer is a son of the King eternal. Erastus kept the city’s treasury and was rich; but his true wealth was that his name was written among the brethren, and among the saved.
webster_summary: An officer of the chamber; a household steward, or the treasurer who keeps the public purse.
webster_full: CHAMBERLAIN, an officer charged with a king’s chamber, or the keeper of a treasury.
From Old French chambrelenc, from Latin camera, “a chamber.”
It denotes a court steward, and also the treasurer of a city or kingdom.
Blastus was Herod’s chamberlain, through whom peace was sought (Act 12:20).
Erastus the chamberlain of Corinth was a brother in Christ (Rom 16:23).
scriptures: And Herod was highly displeased with them of Tyre and Sidon: but they came with one accord to him, and, having made Blastus the king's chamberlain their friend, desired peace; because their country was nourished by the king's country.
Gaius mine host, and of the whole church, saluteth you. Erastus the chamberlain of the city saluteth you, and Quartus a brother.

And he took away the horses that the kings of Judah had given to the sun, at the entering in of the house of the LORD, by the chamber of Nathanmelech the chamberlain, which was in the suburbs, and burned the chariots of the sun with fire.
Est 1:10

On the seventh day, when the heart of the king was merry with wine, he commanded Mehuman, Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha, and Abagtha, Zethar, and Carcas, the seven chamberlains that served in the presence of Ahasuerus the king,
corruption_summary: Not a mere ceremonial title but a real officer of trust — steward or treasurer; the word recovers the stewardship held near the seat of power.
corruption_paragraphs: The honest drift here is toward pageantry. If the modern reader knows the word at all, he thinks of a robed figure in some coronation, a title emptied of substance. But the chamberlain of Scripture is a working officer of trust: the man who governs access to a king, or who keeps a treasury. Blastus controlled the way to Herod, so that whole cities had to court him for peace; Erastus kept the coin of Corinth; the seven chamberlains stood in the presence of the Persian king to do his bidding; even the idolatrous chariots of the sun stood by the chamber of a chamberlain of Judah. The word names men set close to earthly majesty, holding its keys and handling its wealth — a stewardship, not a costume.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the vanity of nearness to earthly thrones and the worth of a name among the saints. The chamberlain stood closest to the king, yet the kings he served were Herod, eaten of worms; Ahasuerus, merry with wine; and the kings of Judah who gave horses to the sun. Proximity to such majesty is proximity to dust. But there was one chamberlain, Erastus of Corinth, whose greatness Paul records not by his office but by his fellowship: he saluteth you, a brother among brethren. He kept the city’s treasury and was a man of rank, but his true riches were laid up where Herod’s worms could not come. The least believer holds a better stewardship than the greatest chamberlain: he keeps the keys of a kingdom that cannot be moved.
roots_summary: The word means an officer of the chamber — a household steward or the keeper of a treasury.

By extension, the treasurer who kept the public “chamber” or purse.
Blastus was Herod’s chamberlain, and Erastus the chamberlain of Corinth.
The seven chamberlains served in the presence of Ahasuerus (Est 1:10).
usage: A chamberlain is a real officer of trust — a steward or a treasurer — not a mere ceremonial title.
Tyre made the king’s chamberlain their friend: to reach the king, one first won the chamberlain.
Erastus the chamberlain of the city was a brother in Christ — his true wealth was among the saints.

etymology: From the Latin magistratus, “a public office, an officer,” from magister, “a master”; hence one clothed with public authority to make and execute law — a civil ruler, a judge, an officer of the state.
biblical_def: A magistrate is a civil ruler clothed with public authority — a judge, a governor, an officer of the state set to make and to execute law. Scripture uses the word for the whole rank of such men, from the praetors of a Roman colony to the appointed judges of Israel. At Philippi Paul and Silas were dragged before them: their accusers “brought them to the magistrates, saying, These men, being Jews, do exceedingly trouble our city” (Act 16:20), and those magistrates, judging in haste and injustice, scourged and jailed them — only to learn their error and fear. Ezra was charged by a Persian king to appoint them for the people of God: “set magistrates and judges, which may judge all the people that are beyond the river” (Ezr 7:25), rulers who knew the laws of God and would teach them. Our Lord assumed the office as an ordinary fact of His people’s life under the nations, promising the Spirit’s help before it: “when they bring you unto the synagogues, and unto magistrates, and powers, take ye no thought how or what thing ye shall answer” (Luk 12:11). Above all the magistrate is the theme of the great charter of civil authority: “Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God” (Rom 13:1). The magistrate does not invent his authority; he receives it. He is the minister of God for good, and a terror to evil-doers — and when he forgets whose minister he is, as the magistrates of Philippi forgot, he answers to the God who lent him the sword.
webster_summary: A civil ruler or judge clothed with public authority — ordained of God as His minister for good.
webster_full: MAGISTRATE, a public officer clothed with authority to make or execute the law; a civil ruler or judge.
From Latin magistratus, from magister, “a master.”
It covers all ranks of civil rulers, from praetors to appointed judges.
The magistrates of Philippi scourged Paul, then feared (Act 16:20).
The powers that be are ordained of God, His ministers for good (Rom 13:1).
scriptures: And brought them to the magistrates, saying, These men, being Jews, do exceedingly trouble our city,
Ezr 7:25

And thou, Ezra, after the wisdom of thy God, that is in thine hand, set magistrates and judges, which may judge all the people that are beyond the river, all such as know the laws of thy God; and teach ye them that know them not.
And when they bring you unto the synagogues, and unto magistrates, and powers, take ye no thought how or what thing ye shall answer, or what ye shall say:
Rom 13:1
Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.
corruption_summary: A civil ruler ordained of God; the word recovers the magistrate as God’s minister, against both anarchic contempt of rule and idolatrous worship of the state.
corruption_paragraphs: Here is a word with a live doctrine to defend, and two errors press upon it from opposite sides. The first is the anarchic temper of our age, which despises all rule, counts every authority a mere social construct, and honours the magistrate only so far as it agrees with him. Scripture will not have it. Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers, for there is no power but of God; the ruler is the minister of God, and he beareth not the sword in vain. To resist the lawful magistrate in his lawful office is to resist the ordinance of God. The Christian is, of all men, the most law-abiding, not from fear of the rod only, but for conscience’ sake, knowing who ordained the office.

The second error is the opposite and equally deadly: the worship of the state, the making of the magistrate into a god who may command the conscience and bind the soul. This too Scripture forbids. The magistrate is a minister, a deputy, a servant holding a borrowed sword; his authority is real but derived, and it does not reach to the throne of God in the conscience. When the magistrates of Philippi scourged innocent men they sinned and were made to fear; when a later Caesar demanded the incense that belongs to God alone, the martyrs died rather than give it. We must obey God rather than men. The magistrate is to be honoured, obeyed, and prayed for — and never worshipped. He is God’s minister, not God; ordained to serve the Most High, and answerable to Him for every stroke of the sword He lent.
roots_summary: The word means a civil ruler or judge clothed with public authority, ordained of God.
roots_lines: Magistrate — Latin magistratus, from magister, “a master.”
It denotes a civil ruler, a judge, an officer of the state.
The office is God’s ordinance: the powers that be are ordained of God (Rom 13:1).
Ezra was charged to set magistrates who knew the laws of God (Ezr 7:25).
The magistrate is God’s minister for good, a terror to evil-doers.
usage: A magistrate is a civil ruler ordained of God, not a mere holder of borrowed power.
The magistrates of Philippi scourged the innocent, then feared: the sword is not borne in vain.
Honour the magistrate as God’s minister, obey him for conscience’ sake — but worship him never.
